title: Your Brain Is Lying
script:
TITLE: Your Brain Is Lying

HOOK: YOU DIDN'T SEE THAT COMING

SCENE 1
VOICE: Your eyes can be wide open, yet your brain can miss something standing right in front of you. And researchers proved it.
VISUAL: text
TEXT: YOU CAN LOOK DIRECTLY AT SOMETHING | AND STILL NOT SEE IT
ICON: eye brain
TONE: mysterious
PAUSE: 0.3

SCENE 2
VOICE: Imagine watching people pass a basketball, while someone in a gorilla suit walks straight through the game. Would you notice?
VISUAL: list
TEXT: WATCH THE BALL | COUNT THE PASSES | IGNORE DISTRACTIONS
ICON: basketball gorilla
TONE: energetic
PAUSE: 0.3

SCENE 3
VOICE: Try this: focus on the players in white, and silently count their passes. Keep your eyes on the ball, not the background.
VISUAL: flow
TEXT: FOCUS ON PLAYERS → COUNT PASSES → IGNORE EVERYTHING ELSE
ICON: eye basketball
TONE: serious
PAUSE: 0.3

SCENE 4
VOICE: Here is the strange part: the gorilla is not hidden, tiny, or especially quick. It crosses the scene in plain sight.
VISUAL: quote
TEXT: GORILLAS IN OUR MIDST | SIMONS AND CHABRIS
ICON: gorilla eyes
TONE: mysterious
PAUSE: 0.5

SCENE 5
VOICE: That is called inattentional blindness. When attention is busy with one task, an obvious event can go unnoticed in psychology.
VISUAL: text
TEXT: INATTENTIONAL BLINDNESS | SEEING WITHOUT NOTICING
ICON: brain eye
TONE: serious
PAUSE: 0.3

SCENE 6
VOICE: In the original experiment, researchers tested one hundred and ninety-two observers across different viewing conditions. The results were surprisingly uneven.
VISUAL: counter
TEXT: 192 | OBSERVERS TESTED
ICON: people clipboard
TONE: serious
PAUSE: 0.4
SOURCE: Simons and Chabris, 1999, Gorillas in Our Midst.

SCENE 7
VOICE: Overall, fifty-four percent noticed the unexpected event, while forty-six percent failed to report seeing it. The gorilla was visible in this experiment.
VISUAL: compare
TEXT: NOTICED | MISSED
DATA: Noticed=54;Missed=46
ICON: gorilla eye
TONE: surprised
PAUSE: 0.5
SOURCE: Simons and Chabris, 1999.

SCENE 8
VOICE: That does not mean people are careless. It shows attention is selective, prioritising what seems relevant to the task in that moment.
VISUAL: flow
TEXT: YOUR TASK → YOUR ATTENTION → WHAT YOU NOTICE
ICON: brain filter
TONE: explanatory
PAUSE: 0.3

SCENE 9
VOICE: Now think about driving. You may scan the road carefully, yet miss a cyclist when your attention is fixed elsewhere.
VISUAL: text
TEXT: LOOKING IS NOT ALWAYS SEEING
ICON: car bicycle
TONE: serious
PAUSE: 0.4

SCENE 10
VOICE: The same limitation can affect conversations. You might hear every word, but miss a facial expression or a change in tone.
VISUAL: list
TEXT: WORDS | EXPRESSIONS | BODY LANGUAGE | TONE
ICON: faces speech
TONE: calm
PAUSE: 0.3

SCENE 11
VOICE: Your brain also fills gaps using expectations. It does not passively record every detail like a camera at any moment.
VISUAL: flow
TEXT: INCOMPLETE INFORMATION → EXPECTATIONS → INTERPRETATION
ICON: brain camera
TONE: explanatory
PAUSE: 0.3

SCENE 12
VOICE: Think of reading a familiar sentence with a typo. Your mind may supply the expected word, so the error slips past.
VISUAL: quote
TEXT: I LOVE EATING CHOCOLATE | I LOVE EATING CHOCLATE
ICON: book eyes
TONE: playful
PAUSE: 0.5

SCENE 13
VOICE: Memory has a similar weakness. Remembering is not replaying a perfect recording; details can shift as we reconstruct an event.
VISUAL: text
TEXT: MEMORY IS RECONSTRUCTION | NOT PERFECT REPLAY
ICON: brain film
TONE: serious
PAUSE: 0.4

SCENE 14
VOICE: That is why confidence alone cannot guarantee accuracy. A vivid memory can still contain mistakes or missing details, even when it feels certain.
VISUAL: list
TEXT: CONFIDENCE IS NOT PROOF | MEMORIES CAN CHANGE
ICON: brain puzzle
TONE: serious
PAUSE: 0.4

SCENE 15
VOICE: Researchers also found task difficulty matters. In their study, people noticed unexpected events more often when the counting task was easier.
VISUAL: bars
TEXT: PEOPLE WHO NOTICED THE EVENT | EASIER TASK VS HARDER TASK
DATA: Easier=64;Harder=45
ICON: brain chart
TONE: explanatory
PAUSE: 0.4
SOURCE: Simons and Chabris, 1999.

SCENE 16
VOICE: Across the easier task, sixty-four percent noticed the event. In the harder task, only forty-five percent noticed it in that experiment.
VISUAL: compare
TEXT: EASIER TASK: MORE NOTICED | HARDER TASK: FEWER NOTICED
ICON: basketball people
TONE: surprised
PAUSE: 0.4
SOURCE: Simons and Chabris, 1999.

SCENE 17
VOICE: So the lesson is not that your senses are useless. It is that attention has limits, especially under pressure.
VISUAL: text
TEXT: YOUR BRAIN IS POWERFUL | BUT NOT PERFECT
ICON: brain lightning
TONE: calm
PAUSE: 0.3

SCENE 18
VOICE: Here is the recap: attention filters what gets noticed, expectations shape what we perceive, and memory rebuilds what we recall.
VISUAL: timeline
TEXT: ATTENTION: FILTERS INFORMATION | EXPECTATIONS: SHAPE PERCEPTION | MEMORY: REBUILDS EXPERIENCES
ICON: brain clock
TONE: energetic
PAUSE: 0.3
SOURCE: Simons and Chabris, 1999.

SCENE 19
VOICE: Next time you are certain you saw everything, pause. Ask what your attention might have filtered out in daily life.
VISUAL: list
TEXT: STOP | LOOK AGAIN | QUESTION YOUR ASSUMPTIONS
ICON: eye magnifying-glass
TONE: serious
PAUSE: 0.5

SCENE 20
VOICE: The biggest twist is this: you cannot notice what you never realise you missed. Stay curious, and check your assumptions.
VISUAL: text
TEXT: THE SCARIEST THING YOU MISSED... IS THAT YOU MISSED IT.
ICON: eye brain
TONE: slow
PAUSE: 0.8

scenes.voice: Your eyes can be wide open, yet your brain can miss something standing right in front of you. And researchers proved it.
Imagine watching people pass a basketball, while someone in a gorilla suit walks straight through the game. Would you notice?
Try this: focus on the players in white, and silently count their passes. Keep your eyes on the ball, not the background.
Here is the strange part: the gorilla is not hidden, tiny, or especially quick. It crosses the scene in plain sight.
That is called inattentional blindness. When attention is busy with one task, an obvious event can go unnoticed in psychology.
In the original experiment, researchers tested one hundred and ninety-two observers across different viewing conditions. The results were surprisingly uneven.
Overall, fifty-four percent noticed the unexpected event, while forty-six percent failed to report seeing it. The gorilla was visible in this experiment.
That does not mean people are careless. It shows attention is selective, prioritising what seems relevant to the task in that moment.
Now think about driving. You may scan the road carefully, yet miss a cyclist when your attention is fixed elsewhere.
The same limitation can affect conversations. You might hear every word, but miss a facial expression or a change in tone.
Your brain also fills gaps using expectations. It does not passively record every detail like a camera at any moment.
Think of reading a familiar sentence with a typo. Your mind may supply the expected word, so the error slips past.
Memory has a similar weakness. Remembering is not replaying a perfect recording; details can shift as we reconstruct an event.
That is why confidence alone cannot guarantee accuracy. A vivid memory can still contain mistakes or missing details, even when it feels certain.
Researchers also found task difficulty matters. In their study, people noticed unexpected events more often when the counting task was easier.
Across the easier task, sixty-four percent noticed the event. In the harder task, only forty-five percent noticed it in that experiment.
So the lesson is not that your senses are useless. It is that attention has limits, especially under pressure.
Here is the recap: attention filters what gets noticed, expectations shape what we perceive, and memory rebuilds what we recall.
Next time you are certain you saw everything, pause. Ask what your attention might have filtered out in daily life.
The biggest twist is this: you cannot notice what you never realise you missed. Stay curious, and check your assumptions.
